turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_te_zt_extrapolation_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Sb, O, Te, Co, Mg, Sn, Se, Pb, Si, S, Cu,
    Ge, Ni, Bi, Ti, Fe, Zn, In, Zr, Ca, Ag, T) and `target` (the measured zT
    measured at each row's own temperature T (K)).
  - b3_te_zt_extrapolation_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE samples whose zT at 800 K
    was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same
    process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST zT at 800
K, then select the 5 best candidates from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
The training data show a clear overall increase of measured zT with temperature and a small number of composition families that already reach zT \(\gtrsim 0.7\) at 500 K.  Because every pool candidate is queried at 800 K, those families are expected to remain the highest-performing after modest further extrapolation.

- Exact match to the strongest 500 K PbTe:Sb point (zT = 1.13) is c043; lightly Sb-doped PbTe analogues sit next (c046).
- The oxychalcogenide BiCuSeO analogue (train zT = 0.76 at 500 K) is c002.
- The best Mg2(Si,Sn) analogue (train zT = 0.70 at 500 K) is c076.
- Unfilled CoSb3 compositions that sit only a few parts-per-thousand from the 500 K point with zT = 0.67 are represented by c054.

All other families present in the pool (GeTe, Cu2Se, half-Heuslers, SiGe, SnTe, \ldots) have distinctly lower 500 K analogues and therefore rank below the five listed above.  The isolated zT = 21.6 point is an obvious outlier inconsistent with both the rest of the data and physical bounds on zT; it is ignored.

Final: c043, c046, c002, c076, c054
